artworks.title: The Daughters of Cecrops Finding the Child Erichthonius
artworks.description: Jordaens' Antwerp canvas shows Cecrops' three daughters opening Athena's forbidden chest — Pandrosos among the sisters who see the serpent-child Erichthonius. In some tellings only Pandrosos obeys and is spared; Baroque painting keeps all three at the moment of discovery.

artworks.title: Daughters of Cecrops Discovering Erichthonius
artworks.description: Rubens' Courtauld sketch returns to the Cecropids and the opened basket — Pandrosos as the eldest daughter to whom Athena entrusted the infant, and whose sisters' curiosity dooms the house.

artworks.title: The Discovery of the Child Erichthonius
artworks.description: Another Rubens treatment of the Athenian crisis: the princesses uncover Erichthonius — Pandrosos' myth as the obedient sister in a story that made Cecrops' daughters Attic household names.

popCulture.title: Pandrosus
popCulture.description: Eldest daughter of Cecrops; Athena entrusts her with the chest holding Erichthonius — later honored with a shrine on the Acropolis beside the olive of Athena.

popCulture.title: Erichthonius of Athens
popCulture.description: The serpent-child Pandrosos was told to guard — Athens' autochthon whose discovery by the Cecropids drives the sisters' myth.
